_link.title: I can describe excitatory and inhibitory effects at the postsynaptic neuron and explain that neither effect is guaranteed

toLevel2.stem: What does an excitatory effect do to the postsynaptic neuron?
toLevel2.answer: Increases the likelihood of firing an action potential
distractors: Guarantees that the neuron will fire an action potential
Decreases the likelihood of firing an action potential
Prevents the neuron from receiving any further signals

toLevel2.stem: What does an inhibitory effect do to the postsynaptic neuron?
toLevel2.answer: Decreases the likelihood of firing an action potential
distractors: Guarantees the neuron will not fire an action potential
Increases the likelihood of firing an action potential
Destroys the receptor sites on the postsynaptic neuron

toLevel2.stem: Why is it incorrect to say that an excitatory neurotransmitter causes the postsynaptic neuron to fire?
toLevel2.answer: It only increases the likelihood, not guarantees firing
distractors: Excitatory neurotransmitters have no effect on firing
Only inhibitory neurotransmitters affect action potentials
The postsynaptic neuron fires regardless of the chemical

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of neurochemicals on the postsynaptic neuron?
toLevel2.answer: They change the probability of firing
distractors: They guarantee a specific firing outcome
They have no effect on firing at all
They permanently alter the neuron's structure

toLevel2.stem: When GABA binds to its receptor sites, what happens to the postsynaptic neuron?
distractors: The neuron is guaranteed to stop firing
The likelihood of firing increases greatly
The neuron immediately fires an action potential

toLevel2.stem: An excitatory effect increases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire an action potential, but firing is not guaranteed.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: An inhibitory neurotransmitter guarantees that the postsynaptic neuron will not fire an action potential.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: An excitatory effect {{blank:1}} the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing an action potential.

distractors: decreases
eliminates

toLevel2.stem: An inhibitory effect {{blank:1}} the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing an action potential.

distractors: increases
guarantees

toLevel2.stem: Neither excitatory nor inhibitory effects {{blank:1}} that the postsynaptic neuron will or will not fire.

distractors: suggest
prevent

toLevel3.stem: Why do excitatory and inhibitory effects only change the probability of firing rather than guaranteeing an outcome?
toLevel3.answer: Multiple signals from different neurons combine to determine firing
distractors: Neurons fire randomly regardless of any neurochemical influence
Each neuron only receives one signal at a time from one source
Neurotransmitters do not actually influence action potentials

toLevel3.stem: How does the correct language about excitatory effects differ from the common student error?
toLevel3.answer: Correct: 'increases the likelihood'; Error: 'causes the neuron to fire'
distractors: Correct: 'causes the neuron to fire'; Error: 'increases the likelihood'
Correct: 'prevents the neuron from firing'; Error: 'decreases likelihood'
Correct: 'guarantees firing'; Error: 'only changes the probability'

toLevel3.stem: Why might a postsynaptic neuron not fire even when an excitatory neurotransmitter binds to its receptors?
toLevel3.answer: Inhibitory signals from other neurons may outweigh the excitation
distractors: Excitatory neurotransmitters never affect the postsynaptic neuron
The postsynaptic neuron can only fire once and then permanently stops
Receptor sites reject excitatory neurotransmitters when they are full

toLevel3.stem: How does the concept of 'likelihood' apply to both excitatory and inhibitory effects?
toLevel3.answer: Both shift probability without determining the final outcome
distractors: Excitatory effects guarantee firing; inhibitory effects guarantee silence
Likelihood only applies to inhibitory effects, not excitatory ones
Both effects determine the exact outcome of the postsynaptic neuron

toLevel3.stem: Which statement best explains why an inhibitory neurotransmitter does not guarantee that a neuron will stop firing?
toLevel3.answer: Excitatory inputs may still outweigh the inhibitory effect
distractors: Inhibitory neurotransmitters have no effect on any neural firing
The postsynaptic neuron ignores all inhibitory signals it receives
Inhibitory effects are always weaker than excitatory effects always

toLevel3.stem: What determines whether a postsynaptic neuron ultimately fires an action potential?
toLevel3.answer: The combined balance of excitatory and inhibitory inputs
distractors: Only the most recent neurotransmitter to bind to the receptor
The size of the postsynaptic neuron's cell body alone
Whether the presynaptic neuron is excitatory or inhibitory

toLevel3.stem: A postsynaptic neuron may still fire an action potential even when it receives an inhibitory signal, if excitatory inputs outweigh the inhibition.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Whether a neuron fires depends on the combined {{blank:1}} of all excitatory and inhibitory inputs it receives.

distractors: sequence
quantity

toLevel3.stem: The common student error is saying excitatory effects '{{blank:1}}' the neuron to fire, when the correct term is that they '{{blank:2}}' the likelihood.

distractors: prevent
reduce
guarantee
determine

toLevel3.stem: A neuron receiving an inhibitory signal may still fire if the {{blank:1}} inputs it receives outweigh the inhibition.

distractors: inhibitory
autonomic

toLevel4.stem: Glutamate binds to receptor sites on a postsynaptic neuron. A student writes: 'The neuron will now fire an action potential.' How should this be corrected?
toLevel4.answer: The likelihood of firing increases, but firing is not guaranteed
distractors: The statement is correct because glutamate always causes firing
The neuron will definitely not fire because glutamate is inhibitory
The neuron has already fired and cannot be influenced by glutamate

toLevel4.stem: GABA binds to its receptor sites on a postsynaptic neuron that is also receiving strong excitatory signals. What is the most likely outcome?
toLevel4.answer: The neuron may still fire if excitatory signals outweigh GABA's effect
distractors: The neuron will definitely not fire because GABA prevents all firing
The neuron will definitely fire because excitatory signals override GABA
GABA and excitatory signals cancel out and nothing happens at the synapse

toLevel4.stem: A VCE exam question asks: 'Describe the effect of an inhibitory neurotransmitter on the postsynaptic neuron.' Which response would receive full marks?
toLevel4.answer: It decreases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing
distractors: It prevents the postsynaptic neuron from ever firing again
It causes the postsynaptic neuron to immediately stop firing
It has no measurable effect on the postsynaptic neuron at all

toLevel4.stem: Liam's neuroscience textbook states that 'excitatory neurotransmitters make the neuron fire.' His teacher marks this as incorrect. Why?
toLevel4.answer: The correct wording is that they increase the likelihood of firing
distractors: Excitatory neurotransmitters actually decrease the likelihood of firing
Neurotransmitters have no influence on whether a neuron fires at all
The textbook is correct and the teacher made an error in the marking

toLevel4.stem: A postsynaptic neuron receives both glutamate and GABA signals simultaneously. Which statement best applies the concepts of excitatory and inhibitory effects?
toLevel4.answer: The neuron's firing depends on the balance of both signals
distractors: Glutamate always overrides GABA so the neuron will definitely fire
GABA always overrides glutamate so the neuron will definitely not fire
The two signals cancel each other out completely every single time

toLevel4.stem: Sophie writes in her exam: 'GABA stops the postsynaptic neuron from firing.' Her teacher deducts marks. What correction should Sophie make?
toLevel4.answer: GABA decreases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing
distractors: GABA increases the likelihood of the postsynaptic neuron firing
GABA has no effect on the postsynaptic neuron's action potential
Her original answer was correct and should not have lost any marks

toLevel4.stem: A researcher observes that a postsynaptic neuron fires despite receiving inhibitory signals. Which explanation best accounts for this observation?
toLevel4.answer: Excitatory inputs were strong enough to override the inhibition
distractors: The inhibitory signals were not actually reaching the neuron at all
Inhibitory neurotransmitters sometimes have excitatory effects instead
The neuron was malfunctioning and firing without any external input

toLevel4.stem: When glutamate binds to receptor sites, the correct description is that it {{blank:1}} the likelihood of firing, rather than saying it '{{blank:2}}' the neuron to fire.

distractors: guarantees
eliminates
prevents
reduces

toLevel4.stem: When a neuron receives both excitatory and inhibitory signals, its firing depends on the {{blank:1}} of these opposing inputs.

distractors: sequence
location

toLevel4.stem: Sophie should correct her answer to say that GABA {{blank:1}} the likelihood of firing rather than saying it 'stops' the neuron from firing.

distractors: increases
eliminates

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that the distinction between 'increases the likelihood' and 'causes to fire' is just semantic and does not matter. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; the distinction reflects a genuine difference in how neurons work
distractors: Correct; the two phrases mean exactly the same thing in neuroscience
Correct; examiners do not distinguish between these wordings at all
Incorrect; the student should say 'decreases the likelihood' instead

toLevel5.stem: Dr Patel claims that excitatory neurotransmitters always result in the postsynaptic neuron firing. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; excitatory effects only increase the likelihood of firing
distractors: Correct; excitatory signals always produce an action potential
Correct; the word excitatory means the neuron will definitely fire
Incorrect; excitatory neurotransmitters decrease the likelihood

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that if a neuron receives both excitatory and inhibitory signals, the two effects always cancel each other out exactly. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; the outcome depends on the relative strength of each signal
distractors: Correct; excitatory and inhibitory signals always cancel each other out
Correct; the neuron always returns to its resting state in this situation
Incorrect; only the excitatory signal matters when both are present

toLevel5.stem: Emma argues that inhibitory neurotransmitters are unnecessary because the brain could simply reduce excitatory signals instead. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; inhibition provides active regulation that reduction alone cannot
distractors: Correct; the brain could function effectively with only excitatory signals
Correct; inhibitory neurotransmitters serve no unique function at all
Incorrect; but only because inhibitory effects are stronger than excitatory

toLevel5.stem: A student writes: 'GABA prevents the neuron from firing, which is why it reduces anxiety.' Which part of this statement requires correction?
toLevel5.answer: GABA decreases the likelihood of firing; it does not prevent it
distractors: The entire statement is correct and requires no correction at all
GABA actually increases the likelihood of firing, not decreases it
GABA has no relationship to anxiety or neural firing at all

toLevel5.stem: Marcus claims that because neither effect is guaranteed, excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters have no real influence on neural activity. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; they significantly influence the probability of firing
distractors: Correct; if effects are not guaranteed they are essentially meaningless
Correct; probability changes do not have any real effect on behaviour
Incorrect; but only excitatory neurotransmitters have a real influence

toLevel5.stem: A researcher suggests that the concept of 'likelihood' is too vague for scientific use and should be replaced with guaranteed outcomes. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; 'likelihood' accurately reflects the probabilistic nature of neural firing
distractors: Correct; science requires absolute outcomes rather than probabilistic language
Correct; neural firing is always deterministic, never probabilistic in nature
Incorrect; but the concept should be replaced with 'possibility' rather than used

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that a single excitatory neurotransmitter binding event should be enough to make a neuron fire. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Unlikely; neurons typically require cumulative input to reach firing threshold
distractors: Correct; one binding event is always sufficient to trigger an action potential
Correct; neurons have a very low threshold that one signal can always reach
Incorrect; neurons never fire in response to excitatory neurotransmitter signals

distractors: correct

toLevel5.stem: The argument that inhibitory neurotransmitters are unnecessary is {{blank:1}} because active inhibition provides regulation that simply reducing excitation cannot achieve.

distractors: correct
